paper_title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/ρ_u$, where $ρ_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $ρ_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

sections.title: 1 The Interaction Problem at Scale
sections.content: Recent advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) (Morris et al., 2024) have largely focused on scaling model capacity, data volume, and computational resources (Sutton, 2019; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), along with innovations in architectures, pretraining or post-training techniques, retrieval, and inference-time search. significant portion of this investment has gone to resource-intensive intelligent system, referred to as System-2, which handles reasoning, planning, decision-making, function calling, or even computer use. As frontier large models (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), extend compute, and larger collectives of agents emerge, the potential of this executive system grows proportionally with resource availability. However, as systems become more capable, the costs of generating, evaluating, and acting on each additional interaction may become constraining factor. This presents an alternative scaling challenge: not merely how many interactions system can manage, but which interactions justify their associated costs. An interaction encompasses any information exchange between an intelligent system and its data, computations, or environment. It gathers information at cost: for large language model (LLM), generation episode in which prompt produces tokens, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022); for an embodied or reinforcement-learning agent, trajectory of states, actions, and rewards; for tool-using agent, tool invocation that calls an external resource and integrates its result. Here, we treat interaction as the unit of analysis, recognizing that these operations are not necessarily equivalent in physical or statistical sense; they share that each incurs resource commitments before observing the outcome and realizes utility only afterward. Even though reasoning models (Guo et al., 2025) and embodied agents (Kim et al., 2024) benefit from increased interactions, the relative returns from each interaction 1 Figure 1 An Illustrative Roadmap to AGI and its Beyond. As AI development progresses, broad capability resembles summit that systems approach but may hit diminishing returns due to constraints in data, compute, and parameters. In Era 1 (20122020) progress came mainly from scaling model capacity, and in Era 2 (20202025) from scaling data and computation. For Era 3 (2026+), this work emphasizes next-scaling lens: co-designing cost-effective System-1 that prioritizes interactions by expected utility and resource-intensive System-2 for complicated tasks. This emphasis becomes increasingly consequential for foundation models and embodied agents as they depend on generation, computation, tool use, and environmental interaction, and thus on the cost of each. tend to diminish. For instance, tokens that fail to alter the relevant belief state, training rollouts that yield little policy-gradient signal under the selected objective (Yu et al., 2026), and environment steps that reiterate known information all consume valuable resources while providing minimal task-relevant learning signals. Determining which interactions to execute is challenge that System-2 cannot resolve autonomously because assessing an interactions value must cost considerably less than executing it. This necessitates the co-design of System-1 and System-2, and this work introduces the conditional interaction as feasible co-design principle: lightweight System-1 predicts the utility of potential interactions, the resource-intensive System-2 executes only those interactions that exceed resource-aware threshold, and the resulting outcomes then serve to refine System-1. Because each system shapes the other, the two must be designed together, and this Perspective asks whether such co-design is promising path toward AGI. Our central hypothesis posits that the density of utility-relevant interactions, denoted as 𝜌𝑢, rather than the sheer count of interactions alone, serves as pivotal metric of scaling efficiency. The co-design of System-1 and System-2, as detailed below, indicates promising approach for scenarios where interactions are costly, exhibit uneven value, and can be anticipated. This framework is based on the premise that low-cost experiments can be conducted and foreseen effectively. The Closing of the Accumulation Frontier. The pursuit of accumulating additional data is increasingly difficult. Human-generated data are finite, since pretraining consolidates much of humanitys recorded text into single model and the stock of public text may be depleted within this decade (Villalobos et al., 2024), while high-quality data are scarcer still, as the subset that teaches most is only fraction of that stock. Synthetic data shift the focus from 2 quantity to coverage: they can partially replenish both (Xu et al., 2025), but the space of synthesizable interactions is combinatorially vast, e.g., robotic data alone would require covering scenes, objects, dynamics, lighting, and sensing, so the pertinent question becomes which synthetic interactions are worth their cost. Moreover, some interactions are inherently expensive: in scientific discovery, robotics, and specialized clinical and industrial settings, data are produced one experiment, actuation, or measurement at time, at the pace of the underlying process, and no amount of computational power can accelerate chemical reaction. Shifting the focus toward continual, post-deployment adaptation, we can find that self-evolution sharpens rather than alleviates the bottleneck: an agent that interacts indiscriminately exhausts its finite budget on experiences that yield minimal task-relevant learning, so its progress hinges on which interactions it selects, precisely the decision this Perspective examines. Conditional interaction aids in predicting which prompts yield non-zero advantage, thereby optimizing the generation budget. The physical regime: expensive rollouts in high-dimensional task spaces. The qualitative insight is that, in high-dimensional spaces, which tasks are evaluated holds equal importance to how many are assessed. The super parrot hypothesis: AI for AI, and its eﬃciency issue. Fig. 2 sketches trend we call the super parrot hypothesis. The early foundation model first behaves as stochastic parrot (Bender et al., 2021), imitating human text without grounded understanding (Stage 1, roughly 20202022); CoT prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and RLVR (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) then let it develop reasoning that humans can still follow (Stage 2, 20222025); and we hypothesize Stage 3 in which it encodes information in self-coded representations and improves itself through self-evolution, beyond human interpretation. Viewed as trajectory, this is trend toward AI for AI: at each stage larger share of what the system learns from is produced by AI itself, synthetic instructions (Xu et al., 2025), self-generated reasoning traces scored by automatic verifiers, and ultimately self-chosen experiments (Silver and 3 Figure 2 The Super Parrot Hypothesis. An illustrative, hypothesized trajectory rather than an established chronology: conceptual progression of AI from imitation-based language learning (20202022), through interpretable reasoning enabled by chain-of-thought (CoT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (20222025), to hypothesized future (2026+) of self-coded representations and self-evolution that may exceed human interpretability. As AI increasingly produces the data and feedback it learns from (AI for AI), deciding which self-generated interactions are worth executing becomes central efficiency problem. Sutton, 2025). The same trend exhibits the efficiency issue in sharper form. Every self-generated interaction is paid for with the systems own compute, yet many of them, such as degenerated RLVR prompts, reasoning tokens that leave the answer unchanged, and self-proposed tasks that are already mastered, teach little to the model. Developing super parrot therefore needs an internal judgment of value before execution, which is precisely the role this Perspective assigns to System-1. All of the above discussions raise fundamental Research Question: How can System-2 be aware of an interactions value before execution? Our position: co-design the two systems, and the conditional interaction decides what the other pays for. In response, we prioritize architecture over algorithm: give the executive partner whose job is to judge, and design the two together. This work argues that major part of the next advance toward AGI and beyond may come from co-designing System-1 and System-2 rather than from scaling System-2 alone: specifying, training, and scaling the two as one system, where System-1 decides what System-2 executes, which executive runs it, how much it may spend, and what it keeps in memory; System-2s outcomes are System-1s supervision; and each is sized with the other in view (Section 3). Integrating cheap predictor with costly executor introduces three decisions at scale: which prompts, tasks, or requests merit rollouts, trials, or extensive thought chains (compute); which samples, buffers, caches, and context entries should be preserved (storage); and how costly outcomes should adjust the inexpensive judgment that allocated them (feedback). This work proposes conditional interaction as coupling mechanism that allocates interactions based on predicted utility, explicitly optimizing to avoid those predicted to fall below certain threshold. What we claim, and with what conﬁdence. Throughout this work, the claim hierarchy is as follows. (i) Premise: future digital and robotic systems may be limited by interaction efficiency more than by parameters or data. (ii) Position: progress toward general intelligence should co-design cheap System-1 with costly System-2, coupled by strategy that values interactions before execution and suppresses those predicted to be uninformative. (iii) Hypothesis: the density of utility-relevant interactions 𝜌𝑢 (𝜌info for information gain) is an important determinant of how efficiently resources become capability. sections.title: 2 Conditional Interaction as A Co-Design Strategy: Predict Before You Pay
sections.content: Co-design requires an interface: precise statement of what System-1 judges, what System-2 executes as resourceintensive operation, and what flows back. Conditional interaction is that interface. Both systems are defined by execution role rather than model family: System-1 is lightweight, semantic-aware module that takes candidate interaction as input, e.g., prompt, task configuration, query, or tool call, with its context and returns score rather than solution, and it is consulted on every candidate at cost 𝑐pred 𝑐exec. System-2 is the resource-demanding model or agent that performs the interaction, and is invoked only on the candidates System-1 certifies. The loop runs in both directions, making it co-design rather than filter bolted onto finished executive: System-1 shapes the data and effort System-2 receives, and System-2s outcomes become System-1s supervision. AlphaZero illustrates this, since its play comes not from deeper search alone but from policy-value network and tree search that trained each other (Silver et al., 2018): more capable System-2 raises the intelligence of accomplishing tasks, while well-calibrated System-1 determines how much of it is reached per unit of cost and latency (See Fig. 3). Static cascades versus adaptive co-design. The pairing can be built in two ways (See Fig. 4). In static cascade, standalone fast model classifies each request and hands the hard minority to large model; Jev, commercial model described by its developers as System One (TypeSafe AI, 2026), is clear instance, returning calibrated probabilities over answers defined in advance (Osman, 2026). Such products illustrate commercial interest in fast, structured judgment models compatible with the System-1 role, although single product does not establish an industry-wide convergence. static cascade is, by construction, trained once, routes only at the inference layer, and does not receive System-2s outcomes, which suffices when its predictions are stationary but fails here, because how informative an interaction is for the current System-2 changes with every update. In co-design, System-1 instead predicts utility such as difficulty or learning value relative to the current System-2; it acts in training as well as at inference, scheduling compute and storage such as rollout budgets, replay buffers, batches, keyvalue (KV) caches, context windows, rather than single call path. System-2s realized rewards, gradients, and outcomes recalibrate System-1 online (See Fig. 5). cascade retrained online on its outcomes moves toward co-design, so the distinction is not the presence of two models but feedback and joint optimization. 6 Figure 4 Static cascades versus adaptive co-design. (a) standalone fast model routes each request once and is never updated by the outcomes. (b) In co-design, System 1 schedules System 2s compute and storage, System 2s outcomes recalibrate System 1, and the two are optimized jointly, so System 1s judgements track an executive that keeps changing. Cascades retrained online on their outcomes lie between the two.

sections.title: 2.4 Scope: When Gating Is and Is Not Justiﬁed
sections.content: The principle applies only where interactions are individually costly, heterogeneous in informativeness, and predictable before execution by model cheaper than execution itself. Gating has no guaranteed advantage when candidates are homogeneous in utility, when predicting their utility costs about as much as executing them, or when execution is cheap. Dense pretraining, minibatch stochastic gradient descent over independent, identically distributed data, and static supervised learning often come close to these conditions, but need not: fixed corpus can hold examples whose value differs and is predictable from cheap features, which data-selection methods exploit. gain observed there calls for an accounting of where it comes from, not refutation of the principle. Within that regime, gating is justified when predictor exists whose cost is well below execution cost and whose error 𝜀 𝜙 is small relative to the utility gaps it must resolve (Theorem 18). It should be relaxed, executing uncertain or even predicted-uninformative interactions, when: (1) the predictor is poorly calibrated or off-distribution, since its blind spots are where it wrongly suppresses; (2) interactions carry option or exploratory value not captured by one-step utility; (3) prediction costs about as much as execution, voiding Theorem 14; (4) false negatives are catastrophic (safety-critical control, irreversible actions); or (5) the utility is misspecified, so that the predictor systematically suppresses the very interactions that would reveal the misspecification. In such regimes the right object is an exploratory value of information, e.g. an upper-confidence or Thompson criterion, replacing ˆ𝑢 in Eq. (15) with ˆ𝑢 + 𝑐 𝜎𝜙, which recovers pure exploitation as 𝑐 0 and uncertainty-seeking exploration, dominated by 𝜎𝜙, as 𝑐 . That limit favours the most uncertain candidates rather than sampling the pool uniformly; undirected exploration needs separate mixture with uniform policy, as in Section 7.2; the uncertainty-aware acquisition functionals of Eqs. (65) and (62) (Section B) are the mechanism by which the principle avoids over-pruning. Conditional interaction is statement about how to spend trustworthy informativeness signal, not claim that one always exists. Regimes (1) and (5) are the most insidious, since the predictors errors concentrate precisely where it has no data and the interactions that would reveal them are never executed; the audit sampling described after Theorem 14 is the minimal safeguard, and Section 7.2 treats this censoring formally.

sections.title: 4 What Prediction Buys, and Why a Small System-1 Can Work
sections.content: Sections 2 and 3 defined the gate and the architecture built around it. Co-design pays only if System-1 is both much cheaper than System-2 and accurate enough to steer it; this section asks when both hold. Section 4.1 states the core formal results: what prediction buys, in time and memory, and the regret cheap predictor risks. The remaining subsections ask why cheap System-1 can make useful prediction about an expensive interaction at all, from three complementary views. These connections are interpretive rather than separate contributions; each supplies insight and, under its own assumptions, guarantee, but none is derivation of the framework. Information-theoretically (Section 4.2), the quantity gated on is expected information gain net of cost, with epistemic action selection as its limiting case. Generatively (Section 4.3), an interaction is transition of world or policy model, and System-1 is an amortized projection of that model onto single scalar, which is why valuation is cheaper than simulation. Control-theoretically (Section 4.4), executing only what the gate admits is receding-horizon control of learner whose own dynamics are still being learned.

sections.title: 5 Conditional Interaction Across Digital and Physical Domains
sections.content: Reasoning-model fine-tuning and embodied-agent training are instances of one abstraction, distinguished by state space, cost structure, and verifier. In both, conditional interaction learns predictor of value from past outcomes and executes the interactions whose predicted value clears the threshold 𝜅𝑡 of Theorem 1. The two instantiations share one predicament finding out whether task is worth training on often costs almost as much as training on it while differing in why. Table 1 summarizes the correspondence together with the test-time and agentic settings.

sections.title: 5.1 Digital and Physical Instantiations in the Literature
sections.content: Digital: from ﬁltering after generation to predicting before it. In RLVR only prompts whose sampled responses disagree carry group-relative advantage, and that band drifts as the policy improves (Qu et al., 2026b). Early methods filter after generating: dynamic sampling in DAPO discards prompts whose groups are uniformly correct or wrong (Yu et al., 2026), and online difficulty filtering keeps prompts of intermediate pass rate (Bae et al., 2026), both paying in full for the rollouts that reveal prompt to be uninformative the execute-then-filter baseline of Theorem 14. Later methods predict before generating: GRESO skips prompts that their reward history marks as likely zero-variance (Zheng et al., 2026); MoPPS tracks each prompts success rate with an online Bayesian posterior and approaches an evaluation-intensive dynamic-sampling baseline with far fewer rollouts (Qu et al., 2026a); DPS, BOTS and PCL model 22 prompt difficulty with hidden-Markov process, Thompson sampling and an on-policy value model, respectively (Mao et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026); and GPS trains one small generative predictor on the shared optimization history to select prompts for much larger reasoning model, improving training efficiency and test-time compute allocation (Qu et al., 2026c). The same move extends beyond prompts, to online batch selection in supervised fine-tuning (Zou et al., 2025), to demonstration selection for in-context learning, where small trained model makes single edit to the retrieved demonstrations instead of iteratively scoring or searching over demonstration subsets (Wen et al., 2026b), to rollout allocation across tasks and trajectory prefixes in agentic RL (Zou et al., 2026b), and to critic-free, tree-aware credit assignment for long-horizon agents (Zou et al., 2026a). These results illustrate rather than validate the framework. Physical: from randomizing to predicting adaptation risk. For embodied agents, judging task configuration means acting on it, on hardware or in high-fidelity simulator, at the pace of physics. Domain randomization trains across wide ranges of simulated appearance and dynamics (Tobin et al., 2017), with an explicit assessment of transfer (Muratore et al., 2018); because uniform randomization spends most trajectories on mastered configurations, later work prioritizes, through active and automatic domain randomization (Mehta et al., 2020; Akkaya et al., 2019) and through environment design and level replay driven by regret or learning potential (Dennis et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021), though still by executing configurations to score them. When robustness matters, the target is the adverse tail of post-adaptation risk, measured by the conditional value-at-risk (Rockafellar et al., 2000) and pursued in robust meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023; Lv et al., 2024), risk-averse planning (Carpin et al., 2016) and safety-critical scenario generation (Rempe et al., 2022). Locating that tail requires evaluating many tasks; MPTS removes the evaluation by learning risk predictive model from the optimization history (Wang et al., 2026), and its successors add posterior sampling and diversity (Qu et al., 2025) and in-context risk prediction (Wen et al., 2026a), yielding curriculum-like sampling under calibrated predictor. What the two literatures share. Evaluation requires generating in the digital regime and acting in the physical one, yet both literatures converge on the same loop: System-1 scores candidate from cheap features and history, System-2 executes only what clears the score, and System-2s outcomes refit System-1. They differ in utility (mixed outcomes versus tail adaptation risk; Theorem 5) and in the conserved resource (compute versus actuation); their acquisition functions are collected in Section B. Unlike post-hoc data valuation by influence functions or data Shapley (Koh and Liang, 2017; Ghorbani and Zou, 2019), and unlike active learning, experimental design and bandit index policies over static pool (Krishnakumar, 2007; Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995; Gittins, 1979), these methods value candidates before execution and track moving learner. They also extend earlier fastslow pairings, such as expert iteration and AlphaZero (Anthony et al., 2017; Silver et al., 2018) and speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), from one game or one decoding step to training and deployment.

sections.title: 6 Conditional Interaction at Test Time
sections.content: The framework so far concerns training. The same decision problem appears at inference, but with different state, utility and cost ledger. Nothing in Theorem 1 and Eq. (9) requires the training setting: the rule gates an interaction on predicted utility net of cost, whether the resource is training rollout or an inference-time forward pass. We argue that test-time scaling and adaptive decision-making, usually studied separately, can be cast as test-time instances of conditional interaction. Prospective metacognitive control of test-time compute is an active line of work in its own right (Nazi and Dipta, 2026; Cao et al., 2026); the contribution here is not to discover it but to place it in the same ledger as training. Assumption (a) fails on long interface trajectories, where dozen individually uninformative clicks may be jointly needed to reach the screen that matters, and whenever locally uninformative action, such as navigating, authenticating or opening file, is prerequisite for useful one; there utility belongs to the sub-trajectory or state transition, valued by state-dependent value of information, and the unit to score is sub-trajectory, and since the accuracy loss grows linearly in 𝑁, the per-action error must shrink with the horizon. Pure exploration (Section 2.4) and mandated actions such as safety logging lie outside the gate. Across Sections 6.1 and 6.2 and this subsection the predictgateexecute pattern is shared while utilities and costs are not  (Table 1)  , so System-1 calibrated against System-2 during training can serve as the inference-time router, with deployment outcomes flowing back as its training data.

sections.title: 7 A Testable Scaling Hypothesis, and Open Problems
sections.content: Co-design makes two kinds of prediction: what the pair should achieve as it scales, and where it can fail. We state the first as testable hypothesis about informative compute, then turn to the main obstacle System-1 is supervised only by the interactions it lets System-2 execute and to open problems. It helps to separate three kinds of claim. Proved under stated assumptions: the IIE accounting (Theorem 7), the screening and memory results (Theorems 14 and 15), the regret bounds (Theorems 18 and 19), the test-time and agentic cost bounds (Theorems 22 and 23), co-scaling under fixed error curves (Theorem 13) and horizontal rescaling (Theorem 24). Supported by application-specific evidence: the savings of predictive prompt and task sampling (Section 5.1). Proposed hypotheses: co-designed frontier that dominates on cost, quality of service and task success at once  (Fig. 3)  , the decay of 𝜌𝑢 (Theorem 25), and changed scaling exponent.

Under perfect gate it is one. With equal costs, as Theorem 24 assumes, the two runs of Theorem 24 accumulate informative compute at rates 𝜌𝑢 and 1. The framework predicts more than constant-factor gain: if the fraction of utility-relevant interactions changes as learner becomes more capable, total compute is not the only meaningful coordinate of scaling, and the question is whether performance curves become more comparable when plotted against Eq. (54). Two hypotheses answer differently and are experimentally distinguishable: the conservative one is that gating produces only horizontal rescaling, the stronger one that it also alters the trajectory of interaction density and thereby the effective exponent. Proposition 24 (Horizontal Rescaling of the Scaling Curve). Suppose (a) unconditional training follows loss curve Lbase (C) on pool whose density of utility-relevant interactions is constant 𝜌𝑢 (0, 1]; (b) dead interactions leave the learner unchanged; (c) progress depends only on the utility-relevant interactions executed, whose distribution and order the selection policy preserves; and (d) the selection policy is perfect, prediction is free, and executions cost the same. Then LCI (C) = Lbase (C/𝜌𝑢) , (56) i.e. on log-compute axis the conditional curve is the unconditional one shifted left by ln(1/𝜌𝑢). This is rescaling identity, valid for any shape of Lbase: it is the precise content of the 1/𝜌𝑢 multiplier used throughout. Assumption (a) fixes 𝜌𝑢, which the next hypothesis denies in general; when the pool fraction drifts, the constant factor becomes the time-varying reparameterization Eq. (54), and that integral is what the curve-collapse test below plots against. Hypothesis 25 (Informative Interaction Decay). After an initial transient, 𝜌𝑢 (𝜃𝑡 ) is non-increasing as the system improves: mastered interactions leave the utility-relevant set, so 𝜌𝑢 tracks the shrinking measure of reachable but not-yet-mastered interactions. 27 The hypothesis is empirical and can fail, since new capabilities can expose new informative tasks and an improved predictor changes what is selected. Its logical direction matters, and it rests on an assumption that the definition of 𝜌𝑢 does not supply. Nothing in Eq. (14) makes relevant interactions equally useful: two prompts with non-zero advantage can produce updates of very different size and direction. We therefore assume constant conditional progress: over the regime studied, unit of utility-relevant compute reduces the expected loss by the same amount 𝜂. Under that assumption unconditional learning is the absorption of informative compute, 𝑑L/𝑑C = 𝜂 𝜌𝑢 (𝜃), and an observed power law corresponds to one particular decay, 𝜌𝑢 = 𝑘 L1+1/𝛼 with 𝛼𝐶 = 𝛼, but it does not follow that 𝜌𝑢 produces the scaling law. Gradient noise, intrinsic dimension and loss curvature generate power-law-like curves too; 𝜌𝑢 is simply the most actionable, since gating intervenes on it directly (Theorem 9). Against informative compute measured as in Eq. sections.title: 7.2 Selective Supervision: The Gate Censors Its Own Training Data
sections.content: The most consequential technical limitation is structural: once System-1 decides which interactions are executed, it also decides which interactions it is trained on. With 𝑝cand(𝑖) the candidate distribution and 𝑒(𝑖) = Pr[𝑖 executed 𝑖, H0:𝑡 ] the gates execution probability, the predictor is trained on 𝑝train(𝑖) 𝑝cand(𝑖) 𝑒(𝑖) 𝑝cand(𝑖), (57) so labels are missing not at random: whether an outcome is observed depends on the predictors own estimate of it, and in the worst case candidate scored as low-value is suppressed, its outcome never observed, and the score never corrected. This is the selective-labels problem of algorithmic decision-making (Lakkaraju et al., 2017), the positivity problem of causal inference, and, under shifting distributions, the label-querying problem of active self-training (Zhou et al., 2022b,a). Three features make it tractable rather than hopeless. Positivity can be designed in, but not by temperature: the indicator in Eq. (3) gives every candidate with ˆ𝑢 < 𝜅𝑡 probability zero at every finite 𝛽, so soft gate only randomizes within the admissible set. Positivity needs an explicit component that reaches the suppressed region: an exploration mixture 𝜋 𝜖 = (1 𝜖) 𝜋CI + 𝜖 𝜋0 with 𝜋0 (𝑖) > 0 on the whole pool, which gives 𝑒(𝑖) 𝜖 𝜋0(𝑖) per draw, or independent audit sampling of suppressed candidates at known rate 𝑎, which gives 𝑒(𝑖) 𝑎. Either way 𝑒(𝑖) 𝑒min > 0. The propensities are known, because the gate assigns them, so weighting the predictors loss by 1/𝑒(𝑖) (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952), or combining that weighting with the predictors own regression in doubly robust estimator (Dudík et al., 2011), gives unbiased estimates of its error on the full candidate distribution. And the audit sample of suppressed candidates (Section 4.1) is exactly such positivity-preserving exploration stream, provided its rate is fixed independently of the predictors scores. What remains open is quantitative: how large 𝑒min must be for the predictors error to shrink while the policy and the candidate distribution drift, how the variance of inverse-propensity weights trades against the screening gain, and whether any rate like Eq. (20) survives adaptive, censored collection. Of all the problems the framework raises, we regard this as the one most in need of theory.

sections.title: 7.3 Open Problems and Outlook
sections.content: The decay profile of 𝜌𝑢 (𝜃𝑡 ) has not yet been measured, and doing so is the cleanest single test of the framework; it would also test mechanistic account of emergence, since sub-skill whose 𝜌𝑢 crosses usable threshold abruptly should appear abruptly. We regard this as the most actionable contribution of this Perspective. Several questions stay open. Because aggressive gating discards informative interactions while permissive gating readmits dead ones, efficiency is maximized at an interior admission rate 𝜌 (𝜀 𝜙), whose characterization sits inside 28 non-stationary bandit problem (Auer et al., 2002), as does its inference-time counterpart, whether halting predictor can reach the accuracy Theorem 22 requires without its own forward pass eroding the savings. Theorem 13 fixes the direction in which System-1 should grow with System-2, and sweeping System-1s size at several System-2 sizes while measuring fp, fn and 𝑐pred would give the compute-optimal split between them. And the framework is single-learner: in agent societies, self-play and debate, informativeness is property of joint beliefs, suggesting relational utility and an informative fraction defined on an interaction graph, since an interaction uninformative to its initiator may inform an observer. We regard this last as the most consequential boundary of the framework. Conditional interaction finally resonates, without being equivalent, with the enactive view of cognition urged for AI by Rafiee and Sutton (2026), building on Varela et al. (2017) and the era of experience (Silver and Sutton, 2025): perception as selective activity, in which an agent acts in order to reveal information. Our utility nonetheless answers to an externally given task and cost ledger rather than the agents own self-maintenance, so we formalize the selective-engagement facet alone. Within that scope, routing tasks to System-2 executives (Section 2.3) extends the gate from data to model selection and Section 6 adds the inference boundary, so fully conditional system, whose data, computation, inference effort and external actions are all gated by co-designed System-1, is promising architecture for resource-efficient intelligence at scale, and the argument strengthens with capability if both Theorem 25 and Theorem 13 hold. Beyond human-level performance (Mulgan, 2016), human data and curricula would no longer say what is worth learning, and system would have to choose its own experiments; its System-1 would then decide what superhuman System-2 learns and does, making the gate major source of efficiency.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: This work poses the perspective that the next stage of progress toward AGI may come from the co-design of System-1 and System-2: cheap System-1 that values each candidate interaction before it is paid for, and costly System-2 that executes only what clears the gate, each trained on the others outputs. Conditional interaction, the predictgateexecuteupdate loop that couples them, applies alike to training rollouts, test-time reasoning and agentic actions, and under explicit assumptions yields screening, memory, regret and co-scaling results. These results motivate the scaling hypothesis of Section 7. Our answer to the research question is therefore qualified yes: the co-design is promising wherever interactions are costly, unequal in value and predictable in advance. The decisive next step is measurement: quantify 𝜌𝑢, compare scaling curves at matched informative compute, and test whether co-design changes more than constant factor.
